1041: Nothing afflicts a person like poverty.
1042: When cruel poverty comes, it takes away both the present and the future.
1043: Hankering poverty destroys at once the greatness of ancient descent and the dignity of speech.
1044: Even in the high-born, poverty produces the fault of uttering mean words.
1045: The misery of poverty brings many more miseries in its train.
1046: The words of the poor are profitless, however sound in thought and clear in expression.
1047: The one reduced to utter poverty is regarded as a stranger even by their own mother.
1048: Poverty that nearly killed me yesterday — must I meet it again today?
1049: One may sleep in the midst of fire — never in the midst of poverty.
1050: The destitute who cling to life live on their neighbor's salt and water.
1051: Beg if you meet those who may be begged of. If they withhold, the blame is theirs, not yours.
1052: Even begging can be pleasant, if what is asked is given without grief to the one who begs.
1053: There is even a grace in standing before the liberal who understand their duty to beggars.
1054: Asking from those who never refuse is almost like receiving from oneself.
1055: The world has givers who never refuse — and that is why some simply stand at their door.
1056: All the evil of begging melts at the sight of those who are far from the evil of refusing.
1057: Beggars rejoice exceedingly at beholding those who give with kindness and courtesy.
1058: If there were no beggars, the deeds of this cool wide world would be like the movement of a puppet.
1059: What praise would givers have, if there were no beggars to ask and receive?
1060: Let the beggar not rage at refusal. The misery of poverty is itself enough to bear.
1061: Not to beg at all, even from the excellent who give cheerfully without refusing, does immense good.
1062: If the Maker of the world made begging a way of life — may He Himself go begging and perish!
1063: There is no greater folly than seeking to cure poverty by begging rather than by working.
1064: The whole world cannot sufficiently praise the dignity that would not beg even in destitution.
1065: Even thin gruel tastes like nectar to the one who earned it.
1066: Nothing is more disgraceful to the tongue than to use it to beg water even for a cow.
1067: A plea to all beggars: if you must beg, never beg of the unwilling.
1068: The unsafe raft of begging splits when it strikes the rock of refusal.
1069: The thought of begging melts the heart. The thought of refusal breaks it.
1070: Saying "no" kills the beggar — but the word returns to kill the refuser too. Where then shall he hide?
1071: The base perfectly resemble human beings. We have not seen such exact resemblance in any other species.
1072: The base enjoy more ease than the good — they never trouble themselves about goodness.
1073: The base are like the gods — they do exactly as they please.
1074: The base feel proud when they see people whose acts are meaner than their own.
1075: The base act from fear — or, failing that, from hope of gain.
1076: The base are like a beaten drum — they unburden to others the secrets they have heard.
1077: The base will share nothing — unless it is pried from them with a clenched fist.
1078: The wise are of use the moment you ask, like the sugarcane. The base are of use only when crushed.
1079: The base bring an evil accusation against others as soon as they see them enjoying good food.
1080: The base hasten to sell themselves as soon as calamity befalls. For what else are they fitted?
1081: Is she a goddess, a peahen, or a girl of this earth? My mind cannot tell.
1082: Her beauty returning my looks is like a celestial maiden coming with an army against me.
1083: I never knew what Death was. Now I see it — eyes waging war with feminine grace.
1084: These eyes that seem to kill all who look are at war with her very innocence.
1085: Is it Death, a pair of eyes, or a gazelle? All three are in her looks.
1086: Her eyes would cause no trembling sorrow, if her cruel arched brows properly hid them.
1087: The cloth covering her firm bosom is like the cloth covering the eyes of a rutting elephant.
1088: On her bright brow alone is destroyed my power that used to terrify the fearless.
1089: Of what use are other jewels to her who is adorned with modesty and the meek looks of a fawn?
1090: Unlike boiled honey, which delights only when drunk, love gives pleasure even to look at.
1091: Two looks are in her dyed eyes — one wounds, and the other is the cure.
1092: A single stolen glance of her eyes is more than half the joy of embrace.
1093: She has looked and lowered her head — and that waters the seed-corn of our love.
1094: When I look, she looks down. When I do not, she looks and smiles gently.
1095: She avoids a direct look at me — glancing, as it were, with half-closed eyes and a smile.
1096: Though lovers speak harshly as if strangers, their words are soon understood.
1097: Little harsh words and cross looks are but the play of lovers acting as strangers.
1098: When I look, the pitying maid looks back and smiles gently — a comforting sign for me.
1099: Both lovers can gaze at each other as if perfect strangers.
1100: When eyes agree perfectly, words from the mouth are of no use at all.
1101: Only in a lover's embrace do all five senses rejoice at once.
1102: The remedy for a disease is something different from it — but for the disease this jeweled one causes, she herself is the cure.
1103: Can even the lotus-eyed God's heaven be as sweet as sleeping in the delicate arms of the beloved?
1104: Whence has she the fire that burns when I withdraw and cools when I draw near?
1105: Every form of joy the soul can wish is found in her embrace.
1106: Her shoulders are made of ambrosia — they revive me with pleasure every time I embrace them.
1107: A lover's embrace is as sweet as a home fed by one's own honest earnings, shared freely.
1108: To ardent lovers, sweet is the embrace that no breath of breeze can enter.
1109: Love-quarrel, reconciliation, and union — these are the joys of those who marry for love.
1110: As learning shows one's ignorance the more one learns, so each meeting with the adorned beloved only creates desire for more.
1111: Flourish, O anicham flower! You are delicate — but my beloved is more delicate than you.
1112: O my soul, fancying that flowers seen by many can match her eyes, you grow confused at the sight of them.
1113: Her yielding form, her kiss, her smile, her heady fragrance — all weapons of her spear-like eyes.
1114: If the blue lotus could see, it would bow to the ground saying, "I can never resemble her eyes."
1115: No festive drums deserve a waist so slight — one that wears a whole flower's stem unbroken.
1116: The stars are confused in their places, unable to tell the moon from the maid's face.
1117: Could there be spots in her face, like those in the bright full moon?
1118: If you can indeed shine like a woman's face, flourish, O moon — then you would be worth loving.
1119: O moon, if you wish to resemble her flower-eyed face, do not appear so as to be seen by all.
1120: Soft as they are, the anicham and swan's down still prick her feet like a thorn.
1121: The moisture on the white teeth of the soft-spoken damsel is like milk and honey mixed.
1122: The love between me and this damsel is like the union of body and soul.
1123: O image in the pupil of my eye, depart! There is no room for my fair-browed beloved.
1124: My fair-jeweled one is the living soul when she is with me — the dying soul when she leaves.
1125: Had I forgotten her bright-eyed one, I would remember you, friend — but I never forget her.
1126: My lover would not depart from my eyes; even if I wink, he feels no pain — so ethereal is he.
1127: As my lover abides in my eyes, I will not paint them — he would have to hide.
1128: As my lover is in my heart, I fear eating anything hot — it would pain him.
1129: I will not wink, knowing my lover would hide himself. For this, the town calls him unloving.
1130: My lover dwells in my heart in perpetual delight — but the town says he is unloving and dwells afar.
1131: For those who, having tasted love, pine for more, there is no cure but the fabled palmyra horse — pursuit past all bounds.
1132: Shame set aside, the tortured body and soul take refuge on the palmyra horse.
1133: Modesty and manliness were mine once. Now mine is only the palmyra horse of unbounded desire.
1134: The raft of modesty and manliness is carried off, alas, by the strong current of desire.
1135: She of the garland-like bracelets has given me the palmyra horse — and the sorrow endured at night.
1136: My eyes will not close in sleep for her sake; even at midnight I think of mounting the palmyra horse.
1137: Noblest of all is the woman who will not cross the bounds, though desire floods her.
1138: Desire itself breaks cover and shows in public — forgetting how chaste and generous she is.
1139: And thus, her heart perturbed, she wanders the public roads.
1140: Even strangers laugh at us to our faces — they have never felt this pain.
1141: The rumour, strangely, has saved my life — and by luck, no one else knows.
1142: Not knowing the worth of her flower-eyes, the town has raised a rumour about me.
1143: Let the whole town talk! What I have not yet won feels already won.
1144: Rumour increases the violence of my passion. Without it, it would grow weak and waste away.
1145: As liquor delights one in mirth, so desire delights me whenever it becomes the town's talk.
1146: It was but a single day I looked on my lover — but the rumour spread like the serpent seizing the moon.
1147: This malady is manured by the talk of women and watered by my mother's harsh words.
1148: To say rumour can extinguish passion is like extinguishing fire with ghee.
1149: He said "fear not" — and left me shamed. After that, why should scandal frighten me?
1150: The rumour I desire is raised by the town itself; and my lover, if I asked, would consent to my following him.
1151: If you are not leaving, say so. If you leave for long — tell it to those who will still be alive to hear.
1152: His very look was once pleasing. Now even union is painful through the fear of separation.
1153: Even the truest lover may sometimes leave — so the heart can hardly rest sure.
1154: If the one who gave his love and said "fear not" should depart — would the fault be with those who believed his words?
1155: If you would save my life, delay my destined husband's departure. Once he leaves, union becomes impossible.
1156: If the hard-eyed one speaks of parting, faint is the hope he will relent and grant my wish.
1157: Do not the rings that begin to slide down my fingers forebode my lord's separation?
1158: Painful it is to live in a friendless town. Far more painful to part from one's lover.
1159: Fire burns when you touch it. But love burns even from far away.
1160: As if it were easy to kill the pain, bear the parting, and live on after!
1161: I would hide this pain from others — but the more I draw on it, the more it swells like a spring.
1162: I cannot conceal this pain — nor can I tell it, without shame, to the one who caused it.
1163: Desire and shame, hung from my soul as on a carrying-pole, press on a body that cannot bear them.
1164: There is indeed a flood of desire — but there is no raft of safety to cross it with.
1165: What will they prove to be when the storm breaks — those who endure sorrow, yet remain within love?
1166: The pleasure of desire is as great as the sea. The pain of desire is far greater.
1167: I have swum the terrible flood of desire but have not seen its shore. Even at midnight I am alone — still I live.
1168: The night that kindly lulls all living things to sleep has me alone for her companion.
1169: The long nights of this season are crueller than the heartless one who torments me.
1170: Could my eyes travel like my thoughts to my absent lord's abode, they would not swim in this flood of tears.
